    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
   261	that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
   262	harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
   263	gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
   264	mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.
   265	
   266	\section{Decision Principle}
   267	
   268	The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
   269	different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
   270	reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
   271	not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
   272	the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
   273	in the theorem statement.

    16	
    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
    20	of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
    21	complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
    22	the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
    23	source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
    24	A proof may be blocked at
    25	an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
    26	hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
    27	theorem
    28	may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
    29	the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
    30	moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.
    31	
    32	The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
    33	boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
    34	contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
    35	input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
    36	gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
    37	advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
    38	must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
    39	source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.
    40	
    41	\section{Basic objects}
    42	
    43	\paragraph{Source theorem.}
    44	A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
    45	source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
    46	the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
    47	documented paper-gap corrections.
    48	
    49	\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
    50	A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
    51	formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
    52	\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
    53	declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
    54	particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
    55	obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
    56	not assume.
    57	
    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
   181	while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
   182	can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
   183	the wrong definition is still upstream.
   184	
   185	When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
   186	protocol.
   187	
   188	\begin{enumerate}
   189	  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
   190	  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
   191	  relating the existing definition to the source object.
   192	  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
   193	  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
   194	  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
   195	  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
   196	  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
   197	\end{enumerate}
   198	
   199	This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
   200	definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.
   201	
   202	\section{Allowed shapes}
   203	
   204	\begin{center}
   205	\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
   206	\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
   207	\hline
   208	Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
   209	Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
   210	proof-obligation hypotheses \\
   211	Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
   212	source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
   213	theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
   214	Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
   215	remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
   216	avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
   217	proof-complete for that theorem \\
   218	Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
   219	Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
   220	Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
   221	source theorem instead of being produced \\
   222	Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
   223	fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
   224	Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
   225	Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
   226	\end{tabular}
   227	\end{center}
   228	
   229	\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}
   230	
   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232	
   233	\begin{enumerate}
   234	  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
   235	  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
   236	  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
   237	  first missing intermediate assertion.
   238	  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,

   866	\subsection{State-dependent distance measure and approximations}
   867	
   868	We make extensive use of a state-dependent distance
   869	between measurements that has been frequently used in the context of
   870	entangled-prover interactive proof systems (see
   871	e.g.~\cite{IV12,ji2015classical}). For $\rho$ a positive semidefinite matrix and $X$ any linear operator define
   872	$$ \Trho(X) = \Tr(\rho X).$$ 
   873	For any two operators $S, T$, define the
   874	\emph{state-dependent distance} between $S$ an $T$ on a $\rho$ as
   875	$$ \Drho(S, T) := \sqrt{\Trho\big( (S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big)}.$$
   876	Based on the state-dependent distance we define a distance between POVMs, given by
   877	summing the state-dependent distance between the square roots of the POVM elements.
   878	Let $\{M^a\}$ and $\{N^a\}$ be two POVMs
   879	with the same number of outcomes, indexed by $a$, and let
   880	$\ket{\psi}$ be a quantum state. Then the state-dependent distance between the POVMs
   881	$M$ and $N$ on $\rho$ is denoted as $\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})$ and
   882	defined as
   883	\begin{align*}
   884	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}) = \Big(\sum_a \Drho\big(\sqrt{M^a}, \sqrt{N^a}\big)^2\Big)^{1/2}.
   885	\end{align*}
   886	While this notation is ambiguous (since the sum over outcomes is not explicitly
   887	indicated), context will always make it clear which notion of $\Drho$ is
   888	intended. We will also drop the square roots in the case of POVMs that are
   889	projective measurements.
   890	
   891	To simplify the notation, let $A^a = \sqrt{M^a}$ and $B^a =
   892	\sqrt{N^a}$. Then this distance can be rewritten as:
   893	\begin{align}
   894	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2 &= \sum_a \Trho\big( (A^a - B^a)^2 \rho\big) \notag\\
   895	               &= 2 - \sum_a \Re \Trho\big( A^a B^a \big),\label{eq:dpsi-1a}
   896	\end{align}
   897	where we  used the fact that $A^a$ and $B^a$ are
   898	Hermitian and their squares sum to identity. If we specialize to the case of projective measurements
   899	with binary outcomes, we get the following relations (here $A =
   900	A^1 - A^{-1}$ and $B = B^1 - B^{-1}$
   901	are the observables associated to the measurements):
   902	\begin{align}
   903	\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2  &= 2 - \Trho\big(A^{1} B^{1} + A^{-1} B^{-1} + B^{1} A^{1} + B^{-1}
   904	                 A^{-1}\big)  \nonumber \\
   905	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4} \Trho\big((\Id + A)(\Id + B)
   906	                 + (\Id - A)(\Id - B) + (\Id + B)(\Id + A)
   907	                 + (\Id  - B)(\Id - A)\big) \ket{\psi} \nonumber \\
   908	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4}\Trho\big(4\Id + 2 AB + 2 BA\big)\nonumber \\
   909	               &= 1 - \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big(AB + BA\big)  \nonumber \\
   910	               &= \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big((A - B)^2\big)\label{eq:dist_observables}    \\
   911	                &= \Drho(A, B)^2. \nonumber
   912	\end{align}
   913	This distance measure has the following useful property:
   914	
   915	\begin{lemma}
   916	  Let $\rho$ be positive semidefinite, $C$ be a linear operator such that $\|
   917	  CC^\dagger\| \leq K$ and $S, T$ linear operators. Then
   918	  $$\Big|\Trho (C S)- \Trho(CT ) \Big| \leq
   919	  \sqrt{2K} \Drho(S, T).$$
   920	
   921	  Likewise, if $\{C_a\}$ a family of operators such that $\|\sum_a C_aC_a^\dagger\|\leq K$ and $\{M^a\}$
   922	  and $\{N^a\}$ POVMs. Then 
   923	  $$\Big|\sum_a \Trho\big(  C_a \sqrt{M^a}\big) - \sum_a \Trho\big( C_a \sqrt{N^a}\big)\Big| \leq \sqrt{K}\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}).$$
   924	  \label{lem:approx}
   925	\end{lemma}
   926	
   927	\begin{proof}
   928	The proof of both results is identical, and uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality;
   929	we show only the proof of the second. Let $A^a = \sqrt{M^a}$ and $B^a = \sqrt{N^a}$. Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
   930	  \begin{align*}
   931	    \Big|\sum_a \Trho\big( C_a (A^a - B^a) \big) \Big| 
   932	    &\leq     \Big|\Trho\Big(\sum_a  C_aC_a^\dagger  \Big)\Big|^{1/2} \Big|\Trho\Big(\sum_a (A^a -      B^a)^2  \Big) \Big|^{1/2} \\
   933	    &\leq \sqrt{K} \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}),
   934	  \end{align*}
   935		as claimed.
   936	\end{proof}
   937	A second measure of proximity that is often convenient is the
   938	\emph{consistency}. As before, let $\{M^a\}$ and $\{N^a\}$ be POVMs
   939	with the same number of outcomes. Then their consistency is defined
   940	as
   941	\[ \CON_\rho(M, N) = \Re \Big(\sum_a \Trho\big( M^a N^a \big)\Big), \]
   942	so that by~\eqref{eq:dpsi-1a} we have 
   943	\begin{equation} \label{eq:condist}\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2 = 2-2
   944	\CON_\rho(\sqrt{M},\sqrt{N}).\end{equation}
   945	 For collections of binary observables $\{A(a)\}$ and $\{B(a)\}$ we use
   946	\begin{align*}
   947	 \CON_\rho(A,B) &= \sum_a \Re \Big( \sum_{c\in\{0,1\}} \frac{1}{4} \Trho \big( (\Id+(-1)^cA(a))(\Id+(-1)^c B(a) )\big)\Big)\\
   948	&= \frac{1}{2}\Re \Big(1+\sum_a \Trho\big(A(a)B(a)\big)\Big).
   949	\end{align*}
   950	%We also use the notation
   951	%$$ \langle A,B \rangle_\psi = \bra{\psi} A B \ket{\psi}$$
   952	%for any operators $A,B$. The following lemma relates the consistency and the state-dependent
   953	%distance.
   954	%\begin{lemma}[Lemma~10 in~\cite{ji2015classical}]

   957	  %\sqrt{N}) = O(\sqrt{\delta})$.

   960	A useful property of the consistency is that if $M$ and $N$ are POVMs
   961	acting on two separate subsystems of $\rho$, applying Naimark
   962	dilation to each of them results in projective measurements $M'$ and
   963	$N'$ and a state $\rho'$ such that $\CON_\rho(M, N) =
   964	\CON_{\rho'}(M', N')$. 
   965	
   966	Given two observables $A$ and $B$, the product $AB$ is an observable
   967	if and only if $A$ and $B$ commute. The following lemma shows how to define
   968	a ``product'' observable $C$ when $A$ and $B$ commute only
   969	approximately in state-dependent distance, such that the action of $C$
   970	on the state is close to $AB$ (and $BA$).
   971	\begin{lemma}
   972	  Let $\rho$ be a density matrix and $A, B$ observables such that
   973	  $\Drho(AB,BA) \leq \delta$ for some $\delta\geq 0$. Let $C$ be the observable defined by
   974	  \[ C = \frac{AB + BA}{|AB + BA|} , \]
   975		 where we use the convention
   976	  that $M/ |M|$ is defined as the identity on the kernel of $M$. Then
   977	  $$\max\Big\{ \Drho(C,AB),\,\Drho(C,BA)\Big\}\, \leq\, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\delta.$$
   978	  \label{lem:jointobs}
   979	\end{lemma}
   980	
   981	\begin{proof}
   982	  It is clear from the definition that $C$ is Hermitian and an
   983	  observable (i.e. all its eigenvalues are $\pm 1$). Evaluate
   984	  \begin{align*}
   985	   \Drho(AB, C)^2 &=  2 - \Trho\Big( \frac{AB + BA}{|AB + BA|} AB + BA \frac{AB
   986	      + BA}{|AB + BA|} \Big).
   987				\end{align*}
   988	 Notice that $AB$ and $BA$ both commute with $(AB + BA)$ and
   989	  hence with $(AB + BA)/|AB + BA|$. Thus the above
   990	    expression simplifies to
   991			\begin{align*}
   992	   \Drho(AB,C)^2   &= 2 - \Trho\Big( \frac{(AB + BA)^2}{|AB + BA|} \Big) \\
   993	    &\leq 2 - \Trho|AB + BA| \\
   994	    &\leq 2 - \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big( (AB + BA)^2 \big) \\
   995	    &= 2 - \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big(2 \Id + ABAB + BABA\big). 
   996	  \end{align*}
   997	  From the assumption,  $\Drho(AB,BA)^2 = \Trho(2\Id - ABAB -
   998	  BABA) \leq \delta^2$. Substituting in the above, we get $\Drho(AB,C)^2 \leq \delta^2 / 2$, as desired
   999	\end{proof}

  1007	\subsection{Nonlocal games}
  1008	\label{sec:nonlocal}
  1009	In the paper we formulate a number of tests meant to be executed between a verifier and $r$ players (sometimes also called provers), for $r\geq 1$ an integer. These tests all take the form of a classical one-round interaction: the verifier samples an $r$-tuple of questions and sends one question to each player; the players each provide an answer to the verifier, who decides to accept or reject. If the verifier accepts the players are said to win the game. 
  1010	
  1011	We call a tuple $(N,\ket{\psi})$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_1\otimes \cdots\otimes \mH_r$ is an entangled state on the joint space of all $r$ players, and $N$ a collection of POVM for each player and possible question to the player, a \emph{strategy} for the players in $G$. Note that we may always assume $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure state and all POVM are projective. 
  1012	
  1013	Given a game $G$ we denote by $\omega^*(G)$ the highest probability of winning that can be achieved by $r$ players sharing quantum entanglement. For a more thorough introduction to nonlocal games in a similar framework as used here we refer to e.g.~\cite{ji2015classical}. 
  1014	
  1015	One of our tests uses nonlocal games as a means to enforce anticommutation relations between a player's observables. Towards this we introduce the following definition. 
  1016	
  1017	\begin{definition}[Anticommutation game]\label{def:ac-game}
  1018	Let $\wg\in (0,1]$ and $\delta:[0,1]\to [0,1]$ a continuous function such that $\delta(0)=0$. 
  1019	A two-player game $G$ is called a $(\wg,\delta)$ anticommutation game if
  1020	$\omega^*(G)\geq \wg$ and moreover there exists questions $q_X,q_Z$ (called
  1021	\emph{special questions}) to the second player and $\{\pm1\}$-valued functions $f_X,f_Z$ defined on the player's set of possible answers to questions $q_X,q_Z$ respectively such that the following two properties hold:
  1022	\begin{enumerate}
  1023	\item {\em Completeness:} There exists a strategy using the state
  1024	$\ket{\EPR}_{AB}^{\ot m}$ for some $m \geq 1$ and projective measurements that achieves the optimal success probability $\wg$, and is uch that measurement operators $\{A_q^a\}
  1025	\in \Pos(\mH_A)$ for the second player satisfy $\sum_a f_X(a) A_{a_X}^a = \sigma_X \ot \Id$ and $\sum_a f_Z(a) A_{q_Z}^a
  1026	= \sigma_Z \ot \Id$, where $\sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Z$ act on
  1027	the first EPR pair and the identity on the remaining EPR pairs. Moreover,
  1028	for every quesion $q$ received by the second player and answer $a$, the projector $A_q^a$ can be written as
  1029	$A_q^a = \sum_j \Pi_j$ where each $\Pi_j$ is the projector onto an eigenspace of
  1030	a tensor product of $\sigma_X, \sigma_Z$ and $\Id$.\footnote{This seemingly ad-hoc condition is needed for the use of the anticommutation game in the Hamiltonian self-test described in Section~\ref{sec:manyprovers}, but not in the Pauli braiding test from Section~\ref{sec:twoprover}.} We call such a strategy an
  1031	\emph{honest strategy} for $G$.
  1032	\item
  1033	Soundness: Let a projective strategy for the players in $G$ be given such that the strategy uses entangled state $\ket{\psi}\in\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and measurement operators $\{A_q^a\} \in\Pos(\mH_A)$ for the second player. Then for any $\eps>0$, provided the strategy has success probability at least $\wg-\eps$ in $G$, there exists 
  1034	 isometries $U:\mH_A \to \C^2\otimes \mH_{A'}$ and $V:\mH_B \to \C^2 \otimes \mH_{B'}$ and a state $\ket{\psi'}\in\mH_{A'}\otimes \mH_{B'}$ such that if 
  1035	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-ac-xz}
  1036	X = \sum_a f_X(a) A_{q_X}^a\qquad \text{and}\qquad Z = \sum_a {f_Z(a)} A_{q_Z}^a
  1037	\end{equation}
  1038	then 
  1039	$$ \big\| U\otimes V \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR}\otimes \ket{\psi'} \big\|\leq \delta\; \text{and}\;
  1040	\max\Big\{ \DIS_{\rho}(X,U^\dagger (\sigma_X\otimes \Id_{A'}) U),\,
  1041	\DIS_{\rho}(Z,V^\dagger (\sigma_Z\otimes \Id_{B'}) V)\Big\}\leq \delta.$$
  1042	\end{enumerate}
  1043	\end{definition}
  1044	
  1045	The CHSH game~\cite{CHSH69} and the Mermin-Peres Magic Square game~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible} are both known to be anti-commutation games. For the former, see e.g.~\cite{McKagueYS12rigidity} and for the latter,~\cite{wu2016device,CN16}. The advantage of the CHSH game is that there is an optimal strategy which only requires a single EPR pair of entanglement. The Magic Square has the advantage of having value $1$, but an optimal strategy requires two EPR pairs. 
  1046	
  1047	\begin{lemma}
  1048	The CHSH game is a $(\cos^2 \pi/8,O(\sqrt{\eps}))$ anticommutation game. 
  1049	The Magic Square game is a $(1,O(\sqrt{\eps}))$ anticommutation game. 
  1050	\end{lemma}

  1058	\section{The linearity test}
  1059	\label{sec:linearity}
  1060	%----------------------%
  1061	
  1062	We state and analyze a variant of the classic 3-query linearity test of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld~\cite{BLR93} (BLR) that can be played with two entangled players. The two-player test is based on the idea of oracularization with a dummy question introduced in~\cite{IKM09}.  Our analysis builds on~\cite{IV12}, who analyze a $3$-player variant. Their proof is an extension of the Fourier-analytic proof due to H{\aa}stad to the matrix-valued setting. We analyze the two-player variant using similar techniques. 
  1063	
  1064	We note that the use of two players, rather than three as in
  1065	the original test, is essential for our applications to
  1066	self-testing. Ultimately we will require the provers to succeed in a linearity test performed in either of two mutually incompatible bases (e.g. the $X$ and $Z$ bases). Two provers
  1067	can achieve this by sharing a maximally entangled state, but there is no {tripartite} state that would allow three entangled provers to obtain consistent answers whenever they measure their share of the state in either the $X$ or the $Z$ basis. (Formulated differently, $\sigma_X\otimes \sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Z\otimes \sigma_Z$ share a common $+1$ eigenvector, the EPR pair; $\sigma_X\otimes \sigma_X \otimes \sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Z\otimes \sigma_Z \otimes \sigma_Z$ do not. This is a manifestation of entanglement monogamy.)
  1068	
  1069	We show the result in two
  1070	steps. First we show that any set of quantum observables satisfying
  1071	linearity relations approximately in expectation can be ``rounded'' to a
  1072	nearby set of observables satisfying these relations exactly. 
  1073	
  1074	\begin{theorem}
  1075	  Suppose there exist observables $\{A(a)\}_{a\in
  1076	  \{0,1\}^n}$ in $\Obs(\mH)$ acting on a state
  1077	  $\rho \in \Density(\mH)$ such that 
  1078		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qblr-0}
  1079		\E_{a, b} \Trho\big( A(a) A(b) A(a+b)\big) \geq 1-\delta.
  1080		\end{equation}
  1081		Then there exists an extended state $\rho' = \rho \otimes
  1082	  \proj{\rm{anc}} \in \Density(\mH\otimes \mH')$ and observables $\{\cA(a)\}$ in $\Obs(\mH\otimes\mH')$ such that 
  1083		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qblr-1}
  1084		\cA(a) \cA(b) = \cA(a+b) \quad \forall a, b \in \{0, 1\}^n\qquad \text{and}\qquad \E_a
  1085	  \DIS_{\rho'} (\cA(a), A(a))^2 \leq\delta.
  1086		\end{equation}
  1087	\label{thm:qblr}
  1088	\end{theorem}
  1089	
  1090	Here, and throughout this paper, the notation $a + b$ denotes the
  1091	bitwise XOR of $a$ and $b$, i.e. the sum of $a$ and $b$ viewed
  1092	as elements of the additive group ${\mathbb{Z}}_2^n$. We call observables
  1093	$\{\cA(a)\}$ satisfying the first set of relations in~\eqref{eq:qblr-1} \emph{exactly linear}.
  1094	
  1095	\begin{proof}
  1096	For every $u\in\{0,1\}^n$ consider the Fourier transform  $\hat{A}^u =
  1097	\E_{a} (-1)^{a\cdot u} A(a)$. Define measurement operators
  1098	  $B^u = (\hat{A}^u)^2$.
  1099	By Parseval's identity, these operators form a POVM. Using Naimark's theorem there exists an ancilla space $\mH'$, $\proj{\rm anc}\in\Density(\mH')$, and a projective
  1100	measurement $\{C^u\}$ on $\mH\otimes \mH'$ that simulates $\{B^u\}$. Introduce 
  1101	observables
  1102	\[ \cA(a) = \sum_{u} (-1)^{u\cdot a} C^u. \]
  1103	From the orthogonality of the projectors $C^u$ it follows that $\cA(a)
  1104	\cA(b) = \cA(a+b)$. Write 
  1105	\begin{align*}

    66	\section{Combined point measurements}
    67	
    68	The measurements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}$ and
    69	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}$ commute only approximately. The first goal of
    70	this chapter is to construct a single projective measurement that
    71	simultaneously measures both, first at points and then along lines. The
    72	construction of the combined point measurement proceeds in three steps: the
    73	binary refinements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}$ and
    74	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}$ are combined into a sandwich POVM, the
    75	resulting family is shown to satisfy an approximate linearity in the index
    76	pair $(r,s)$, and the following result of Natarajan and
    77	Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity} converts approximate linearity into exact
    78	linearity, from which a projective measurement with outcomes in $\F_q^2$ is
    79	assembled by Fourier averaging.

   104	\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
   105		\label{thm:linearity}

   111		Let $t$ be a positive integer and $\delta \ge 0$. Let $\rho$ be a
   112		density operator on a Hilbert space $\hilb$ and let
   113		$\{\mathcal{O}^u\}$ be a set of binary observables indexed by
   114		$u \in \F_2^t$ acting on $\hilb$, such that on average over $u, u'$
   115		chosen uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$,
   116		\[
   117			\E_{u,u'} \Re \Tr\big(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'} \,
   118			\mathcal{O}^{u+u'} \, \rho\big) \ge 1 - \delta\,.
   119		\]
   120		Then there exist a Hilbert space $\hilb'$, a pure state
   121		$\ket{\mathrm{anc}} \in \hilb'$, and binary observables
   122		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
   123		$\hilb \ot \hilb'$ such that, writing
   124		$\rho' = \rho \ot \ket{\mathrm{anc}}\bra{\mathrm{anc}}$, the exact
   125		linearity
   126		\[
   127			\mathcal{L}^u \, \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}
   128		\]
   129		holds for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, and
   130		\[
   131			\E_{u} \, d_{\rho'}\big(\mathcal{L}^u,\ \mathcal{O}^u \ot
   132			\Id_{\hilb'}\big)^2 \le 2\delta\,,
   133		\]
   134		where the expectation is over $u$ chosen uniformly at random from
   135		$\F_2^t$ and
   136		$d_{\sigma}(S,T)
   137		= \big(\Tr\big((S-T)^\dagger (S-T)\, \sigma\big)\big)^{1/2}$
   138		denotes the state-dependent distance with respect to a density
   139		operator $\sigma$. Equivalently, in the distance $d^{\mathrm{bin}}_\sigma$
   140		between the binary projective measurements associated with the
   141		observables (Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-measurement-distance}),
   142		\[
   143			\E_{u} \, d^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\rho'}\big(\mathcal{L}^u,\
   144			\mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id_{\hilb'}\big)^2 \le \delta\,.
   145		\]

   147		$2\delta$; that normalization is false, and the bounds stated here are
   148		the ones its argument establishes
   149		(Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-distance-normalization}).

   151	\begin{proof}
   152		\leanok
   153		\uses{lem:binary-measurement-distance, lem:blr-defect-identity,
   154			lem:boolean-representation-stability}
   155		This is Theorem~10 of Natarajan and Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity},
   156		whose Fourier--Naimark argument is followed; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} invokes
   157		the result without proof. Write $\chi_v(u) = (-1)^{v \cdot u}$ and
   158		$\widehat{\mathcal{O}}^v = \E_u \, \chi_v(u) \, \mathcal{O}^u$ as in
   159		Lemma~\ref{lem:boolean-fourier-transform}.
   160	
   161		\emph{From the correlation to the multiplicative defect.} For
   162		$u, u' \in \F_2^t$, expanding
   163		$(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'} - \mathcal{O}^{u+u'})^\dagger
   164		(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'} - \mathcal{O}^{u+u'})$ with
   165		$(\mathcal{O}^w)^2 = \Id$ and $\Tr \rho = 1$, as in the proof of
   166		Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-measurement-distance}, gives
   167		\[
   168			d_\rho\big(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'}, \mathcal{O}^{u+u'}\big)^2
   169			= 2 - 2 \Re \Tr\big(\mathcal{O}^{u'} \mathcal{O}^u
   170			\mathcal{O}^{u'+u} \rho\big)\,,
   171		\]
   172		the two cross terms being adjoint to each other. Exchanging the two
   173		coordinates of the uniform pair $(u,u')$, the hypothesis yields
   174		$\E_{u,u'} d_\rho(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'},
   175		\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})^2 \le 2\delta$. No commutation among the
   176		observables is used.
   177	
   178		\emph{The Fourier-square measurement and its Naimark rounding.} By
   179		Lemma~\ref{lem:boolean-fourier-transform} the operators
   180		$B^v = (\widehat{\mathcal{O}}^v)^2$ are positive semidefinite and sum to
   181		$\Id$, so they form a POVM indexed by $\F_2^t$.
   182		Lemma~\ref{lem:naimark-helper}, applied with an ancillary space $\hilb'$
   183		of dimension $2^t + 1$ and with $\ket{\mathrm{anc}}$ the basis vector of
   184		its extra direction, produces orthogonal projectors on $\hilb \ot \hilb'$
   185		compressing along $\ket{\mathrm{anc}}$ to the $B^v$; the residual
   186		projector of the construction is folded into the outcome $v = 0$, which
   187		gives a projective measurement $\{C^v\}$ resolving the identity on
   188		$\hilb \ot \hilb'$ whose compression is still $\{B^v\}$, because the
   189		$B^v$ themselves sum to $\Id$. Set
   190		$\mathcal{L}^u = \sum_v \chi_v(u) \, C^v$. Each $\mathcal{L}^u$ is
   191		Hermitian, and the orthogonality of the $C^v$ together with
   192		$\chi_v(u) \chi_v(u') = \chi_v(u+u')$ gives
   193		$\mathcal{L}^u \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}$ for all $u, u'$;
   194		in particular $(\mathcal{L}^u)^2 = \mathcal{L}^0 = \sum_v C^v = \Id$,
   195		so the $\mathcal{L}^u$ are binary observables.
   196	
   197		\emph{The distance/defect identity.} Since $\mathcal{L}^u$ and
   198		$\mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id$ are binary observables and $\rho'$ is a density
   199		operator, Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-measurement-distance} gives
   200		$d_{\rho'}(\mathcal{L}^u, \mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id)^2
   201		= 2 - 2 \Re \Tr(\mathcal{L}^u (\mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id) \rho')$.
   202		Compressing along $\ket{\mathrm{anc}}$,
   203		$\Re \Tr(\mathcal{L}^u (\mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id) \rho')
   204		= \Re \Tr(\mathcal{O}^u \sum_v \chi_v(u) B^v \rho)$; averaging over $u$
   205		turns $\E_u \chi_v(u) \mathcal{O}^u$ into $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}^v$, and
   206		expanding the three Fourier coefficients and summing the characters
   207		(Lemma~\ref{lem:boolean-fourier-transform}) gives
   208		\[
   209			\E_u \Re \Tr\big(\mathcal{L}^u (\mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id) \rho'\big)
   210			= \sum_v \Re \Tr\big((\widehat{\mathcal{O}}^v)^3 \rho\big)
   211			= \E_{u,u'} \Re \Tr\big(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'}
   212			\mathcal{O}^{u+u'} \rho\big)\,.
   213		\]
   214		Hence
   215		$\E_u d_{\rho'}(\mathcal{L}^u, \mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id)^2
   216		= 2 - 2 \E_{u,u'} \Re \Tr(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'}
   217		\mathcal{O}^{u+u'} \rho)
   218		= \E_{u,u'} d_\rho(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'},
   219		\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})^2 \le 2\delta$ by the first step. The measurement
   220		form follows by halving, through the normalization identity of
   221		Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-measurement-distance}.

   223		The obligations attached to the theorem at its point of use --- the
   224		correspondence between the correlation hypothesis above and the relation
   225		$\approx_\delta$ of Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance}, the
   226		instantiation of $\rho$ as a reduced state of $\ket{\hat\psi}$, the
   227		absorption of the ancilla register into padding of the strategy state,
   228		and the identity $\mathcal{L}^0 = \Id$ --- are enumerated in
   229		Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-import} and addressed in the proof of
   230		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}.
   231	\end{proof}

   233	\begin{remark}[Obligations of the linearity-theorem import]
   234		\label{rem:linearity-import}
   235		Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} is stated in the form established by the
   236		argument of \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, with the normalization of its
   237		distance bound corrected as described in
   238		Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-distance-normalization}. Three features are
   239		load-bearing for the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the error is
   240		preserved without polynomial loss ($\delta$ in the hypothesis becomes
   241		$2\delta$ in the conclusion for the squared operator distance, and
   242		$\delta$ for the squared measurement distance, a constant factor absorbed
   243		by the relation $\approx_\delta$); the linearity of the
   244		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ is exact and holds for all pairs $(u,u')$, not merely
   245		on average; and the hypothesis carries no upper bound on $\delta$, so the
   246		theorem may be applied separately for each pair $(x,z)$ with hypothesis
   247		error the conditional linearity defect given $(x,z)$, a quantity for
   248		which no a priori bound is available. The closeness of $\mathcal{L}^u$ to
   249		$\mathcal{O}^u$ is guaranteed on average over a uniformly random $u$
   250		only; this averaged form suffices because the $\mathcal{L}^u$ enter
   251		the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10} only through averages over $u$.
   252		The quotation of the theorem in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} differs from the
   253		cited statement in three respects: it inserts the restriction
   254		$0 \le \delta \le 1$, which would block the fiberwise application
   255		just described; it places the closeness conclusion, together with the
   256		exact linearity, under the quantifier ``for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$'',
   257		a strengthening of the theorem proved in
   258		\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}; and it appends the identity
   259		$\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ for $u = 0$. None of the three is reproduced
   260		here: the restriction is dropped, the pointwise closeness is not
   261		used, and the appended identity is instead derived from the
   262		conclusion, since exact linearity at $u = u' = 0$ gives
   263		$(\mathcal{L}^0)^2 = \mathcal{L}^0$, and an idempotent unitary equals
   264		the identity. The import carries two conversion obligations,
   265		discharged in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the theorem is
   266		instantiated with $\rho$ the reduced density operator of
   267		$\ket{\hat\psi}$ on the registers carrying the observables, so that
   268		traces against $\rho$ are expectation values in $\ket{\hat\psi}$; and
   269		the correlation hypothesis and the squared-distance conclusion are
   270		converted to and from the relation $\approx_\delta$ of
   271		Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance} by expanding the square, using
   272		unitarity of the observables, and relabelling the averaged index
   273		pair, at the cost of the constant factors absorbed by that
   274		definition. One obligation remains open and is flagged where it
   275		arises: the ancilla register $\hilb'$ and its state
   276		$\ket{\mathrm{anc}}$ produced by the theorem, which may depend on the
   277		pair $(x,z)$, must be absorbed --- uniformly in $(x,z)$ --- into
   278		zero-state padding of the strategy state, padding that the source
   279		assumes present without construction.
   280	\end{remark}

    55	/-- **Partial isometry to unitary extension** (general fact).
    56	
    57	If `V†V = P` where `P` is a projection and `V = VP`, then there exists
    58	a unitary `U` on the full space with `UP = V`.
    59	
    60	This is a standard result in finite-dimensional linear algebra: V is an
    61	isometry from range(P) to V's range, and in finite dimensions any
    62	isometry between subspaces extends to a unitary.
    63	
    64	**Mathlib route**: `LinearIsometry.extend` provides the extension for
    65	linear isometries between inner product spaces. The gap is the
    66	matrix-to-`EuclideanSpace` transport. -/
    67	private lemma partialIsometry_to_unitary
    68	    {n : Type*} [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n]
    69	    (V P : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n)
    70	    (hP : MIPStarRE.Quantum.IsProj P)
    71	    (hVP : V * P = V)
    72	    (hVV : Vᴴ * V = P) :
    73	    ∃ U : Matrix.unitaryGroup n ℂ,
    74	      (U : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n) * P = V := by
    75	  classical
    76	  have toEuclideanLin_mul :
    77	      ∀ A B : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n,
    78	        Matrix.toEuclideanLin (A * B) =
    79	          (Matrix.toEuclideanLin A).comp (Matrix.toEuclideanLin B) := by
    80	    intro A B
    81	    simp [Matrix.toEuclideanLin, Matrix.toLpLin_mul_same (p := (2 : ENNReal)) A B]
    82	  let Pₗ : EuclideanSpace ℂ n →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n := Matrix.toEuclideanLin P
    83	  let Vₗ : EuclideanSpace ℂ n →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n := Matrix.toEuclideanLin V
    84	  let S : Submodule ℂ (EuclideanSpace ℂ n) := LinearMap.range Pₗ
    85	  letI : InnerProductSpace ℂ S := Submodule.innerProductSpace S
    86	  have hP_fix : ∀ x : S, Pₗ (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) = x := by
    87	    intro x
    88	    rcases x.2 with ⟨y, hy⟩
    89	    rw [← hy]
    90	    calc
    91	      Pₗ (Pₗ y) = (Pₗ.comp Pₗ) y := rfl
    92	      _ = Matrix.toEuclideanLin (P * P) y := by rw [toEuclideanLin_mul]
    93	      _ = Pₗ y := by rw [hP.isIdempotentElem.eq]
    94	  have hVP_lin : Vₗ.comp Pₗ = Vₗ := by
    95	    calc
    96	      Vₗ.comp Pₗ = Matrix.toEuclideanLin (V * P) := by rw [toEuclideanLin_mul]
    97	      _ = Vₗ := by rw [hVP]
    98	  have hgram : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Vᴴ * V) = Pₗ := by
    99	    calc
   100	      Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Vᴴ * V) = Matrix.toEuclideanLin P := by rw [hVV]
   101	      _ = Pₗ := rfl
   102	  let Llin : S →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n := Vₗ.comp S.subtype
   103	  have hLnorm : ∀ x : S, ‖Llin x‖ = ‖x‖ := by
   104	    exact (LinearMap.norm_map_iff_inner_map_map
   105	      (𝕜 := ℂ) (E := S) (E' := EuclideanSpace ℂ n)
   106	      (F := S →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n) Llin).2 fun x y => by
   107	      have hy : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Vᴴ * V) (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) = y := by
   108	        calc
   109	          Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Vᴴ * V) (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) =
   110	              Pₗ (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) := by rw [hgram]
   111	          _ = y := hP_fix y
   112	      calc
   113	        inner ℂ (Llin x) (Llin y) =
   114	            inner ℂ (Vₗ (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ n)) (Vₗ (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n)) := rfl
   115	        _ = inner ℂ (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ n)
   116	            (Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Vᴴ * V) (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n)) := by
   117	          dsimp [Vₗ]
   118	          rw [Matrix.toEuclideanLin_conjTranspose_mul_self]
   119	          exact (LinearMap.adjoint_inner_right (𝕜 := ℂ)
   120	            (Matrix.toEuclideanLin V) (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ n)
   121	            (Matrix.toEuclideanLin V (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n))).symm
   122	        _ = inner ℂ (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) (y : EuclideanSpace ℂ n) := by rw [hy]
   123	        _ = inner ℂ x y := rfl
   124	  let L : S →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n := { toLinearMap := Llin, norm_map' := hLnorm }
   125	  let Ulin : EuclideanSpace ℂ n →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n :=
   126	    LinearIsometry.extend (𝕜 := ℂ) (V := EuclideanSpace ℂ n) (S := S) L
   127	  let Umat : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n :=
   128	    Matrix.toEuclideanLin.symm Ulin.toLinearMap
   129	  have hUmat_lin : Matrix.toEuclideanLin Umat = Ulin.toLinearMap := by
   130	    exact Matrix.toEuclideanLin.apply_symm_apply Ulin.toLinearMap
   131	  have hUstarU : Umatᴴ * Umat = 1 := by
   132	    apply Matrix.toEuclideanLin.injective
   133	    calc
   134	      Matrix.toEuclideanLin (Umatᴴ * Umat) =
   135	          (Matrix.toEuclideanLin Umat).adjoint.comp (Matrix.toEuclideanLin Umat) := by
   136	            rw [Matrix.toEuclideanLin_conjTranspose_mul_self]
   137	      _ = Ulin.toLinearMap.adjoint.comp Ulin.toLinearMap := by rw [hUmat_lin]
   138	      _ = 1 := by exact Ulin.adjoint_comp_self'
   139	      _ = Matrix.toEuclideanLin (1 : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n) := by
   140	            rw [Matrix.toEuclideanLin, Matrix.toLpLin_one]
   141	            rfl
   142	  let U : Matrix.unitaryGroup n ℂ := ⟨Umat, (Matrix.mem_unitaryGroup_iff').2 hUstarU⟩
   143	  refine ⟨U, ?_⟩
   144	  apply Matrix.toEuclideanLin.injective
   145	  apply LinearMap.ext
   146	  intro x
   147	  have hExt : Ulin (Pₗ x) = Vₗ (Pₗ x) := by
   148	    simpa [Ulin, L, Llin] using
   149	      (LinearIsometry.extend_apply L ⟨Pₗ x, LinearMap.mem_range_self Pₗ x⟩)

   151	    Matrix.toEuclideanLin ((U : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op n) * P) x =
   152	        Matrix.toEuclideanLin Umat (Pₗ x) := by
   153	          rw [toEuclideanLin_mul]
   154	          rfl
   155	    _ = Ulin (Pₗ x) := by
   156	          rw [hUmat_lin]
   157	          rfl
   158	    _ = Vₗ (Pₗ x) := hExt
   159	    _ = Vₗ x := by
   160	          have hx := congrArg
   161	            (fun f : EuclideanSpace ℂ n →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ n => f x) hVP_lin
   162	          simpa [LinearMap.comp_apply] using hx
   163	    _ = Matrix.toEuclideanLin V x := rfl

   219	For any submeasurement `M : Submeasurement α d`, there exists a projective

   246	  supported only on the input `none = ⊥` slice.

    24	\section{At a glance}
    25	
    26	\begin{itemize}
    27	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The factor-of-two calculation is
    28	  elementary, but the counterexample must remain valid after the ancillary
    29	  extension allowed by the theorem.
    30	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The formal adapter consists of one binary
    31	  effect definition and two distance identities, requiring roughly 70--100
    32	  lines of matrix algebra.  The source-facing theorem is stated with the
    33	  corrected bound.
    34	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} About 60\% is direct finite-matrix and
    35	  finite-sum algebra; the remaining 40\% is the project-local Boolean Fourier
    36	  and state-dependent distance interface.
    37	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs.} Finite sums on the Boolean cube, complex
    38	  matrices and conjugate transpose, cyclicity of trace, and simultaneous
    39	  spectral decomposition for commuting Hermitian matrices.
    40	\end{itemize}
    41	
    42	\section{Key theorem forms}
    43	
    44	Let $S$ and $T$ be binary observables and let $\rho$ be a positive
    45	semidefinite operator of trace one.  We distinguish the state-dependent
    46	operator distance from the distance between their associated binary projective
    47	measurements:
    48	\begin{align*}
    49	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    50	    &:= \Re\tr\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big), \\
    51	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    52	    &:= \sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}
    53	      \Re\tr\big((P_S^s-P_T^s)^\dagger
    54	                       (P_S^s-P_T^s)\rho\big),
    55	  \qquad P_S^\pm := \frac{\Id\pm S}{2}.
    56	\end{align*}
    57	The normalization and correlation identities are
    58	\begin{align}
    59	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2 &= \frac12 d_\rho(S,T)^2,
    60	    \tag{normalization}\label{eq:normalization}\\
    61	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    62	    &= 2-2\Re\tr(ST\rho),
    63	    \tag{operator correlation}\label{eq:operator-correlation}\\
    64	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    65	    &= 1-\Re\tr(ST\rho).
    66	    \tag{binary correlation}\label{eq:binary-correlation}
    67	\end{align}
    68	Consequently, the conclusion delivered by the quantum linearity argument can
    69	be written either as
    70	\[
    71	  \mathbb E_a\dbin_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq\delta
    72	\]
    73	or, equivalently, as
    74	\[
    75	  \mathbb E_a d_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq2\delta.
    76	\]
    77	These are not equivalent to the same bound $\delta$ for the mean squared
    78	state-dependent operator distance.%
    79	\footnote{The formal declarations are \leanid{binaryObservableEffect},
    80	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq},
    81	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_stateDepDistSq\_div\_two},
    82	\leanid{stateDepDistSq\_eq\_two\_sub\_two\_mul\_correlation}, and
    83	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_one\_sub\_correlation} in
    84	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity/BooleanFourier.lean}.}
    85	
    86	\section{The source calculation}
    87	
    88	Natarajan and Vidick define the distance between two POVMs by summing the
    89	squared state-dependent distances between corresponding square roots
    90	\cite[Section~3.1]{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  For projective measurements the
    91	square roots are the effects themselves.  In the binary case their calculation
    92	expands $P_S^\pm=(\Id\pm S)/2$ and obtains
    93	\[
    94	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    95	    = 1-\frac12\tr_\rho(ST+TS)
    96	    = \frac12\tr_\rho((S-T)^2).
    97	  \tag{source equation (3)}
    98	\]
    99	This is equation~(3) at lines~903--910 of the in-repository source mirror.%
   100	\footnote{See
   101	\path{references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex}, lines~866--912.  The quantum
   102	linearity theorem and its Fourier--Naimark proof are at lines~1074--1112.}
   103	The next line identifies the final expression with the squared state-dependent
   104	operator distance.  The operator-distance definition at lines~873--875 is
   105	printed with $\rho$ occurring twice,
   106	\[
   107	  d_\rho(S,T)^2 = \tr_\rho\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big),
   108	  \qquad \tr_\rho(X) := \tr(\rho X),
   109	\]
   110	and we read the duplication as typographical, keeping the single $\rho$ of the
   111	definition of $d$ above.  Under that reading the squared state-dependent
   112	operator distance is $\tr_\rho((S-T)^2)$ rather than one half of that
   113	quantity.  Thus the calculation through line~910 is correct and the equality
   114	on line~911 loses a factor of two.
   115	
   116	The Fourier--Naimark proof is consistent with the measurement normalization.
   117	It proves
   118	\[
   119	  \mathbb E_a\operatorname{CON}_{\rho'}(A(a),\mathcal A(a))
   120	  = \frac12+\frac12\mathbb E_{a,b}
   121	       \tr_\rho(A(a)A(b)A(a+b)).
   122	\]
   123	The hypothesis therefore makes the consistency deficit at most $\delta/2$.
   124	For binary projective measurements, the squared measurement distance is twice
   125	that deficit, giving the bound $\delta$ for the squared binary-measurement
   126	distance and the bound $2\delta$ for the squared state-dependent operator
   127	distance.

   129	\section{A four-point counterexample}
   130	
   131	The bound $\delta$ for the mean squared state-dependent operator distance is
   132	false.  Let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$, choose $r\in G\setminus\{0\}$, take
   133	the one-dimensional state $\rho=1$, and define scalar binary observables by
   134	\[
   135	  A(a)=\begin{cases}
   136	    -1,&a=r,\\
   137	     1,&a\neq r.
   138	  \end{cases}
   139	\]
   140	For the characters $\chi_u(a)=(-1)^{u\cdot a}$, the normalized Fourier
   141	coefficients satisfy
   142	\[
   143	  \widehat A(0)=\frac12,
   144	  \qquad
   145	  \widehat A(u)=-\frac12\chi_u(r)\quad(u\neq0).
   146	\]
   147	Their multiset is
   148	$\{\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12\}$, and hence
   149	\[
   150	  \mathbb E_{a,b}A(a)A(b)A(a+b)
   151	    =\sum_u\widehat A(u)^3=\frac14.
   152	\]
   153	The correlation hypothesis therefore holds with $\delta=3/4$.
   154	
   155	Every scalar exact Boolean representation is one of the characters $\chi_u$,
   156	and its mean squared state-dependent operator distance from $A$ is
   157	\[
   158	  \mathbb E_a |A(a)-\chi_u(a)|^2
   159	    =2-2\widehat A(u)\geq1.
   160	\]
   161	Allowing an ancillary space does not reduce this lower bound.  Exact linearity
   162	and the binary-observable relations make the operators $\mathcal A(a)$ a
   163	commuting family of Hermitian involutions.  Their simultaneous spectral
   164	subspaces carry characters of $G$.  Evaluation in any density operator is
   165	therefore a convex combination of the scalar character correlations above, so
   166	the mean squared state-dependent operator distance remains at least $1$.  It
   167	cannot be at most $\delta=3/4$.  By~\eqref{eq:normalization}, the corresponding
   168	mean squared binary-measurement distance has lower bound $1/2$, which is
   169	compatible with the provider's conclusion.

   866	\subsection{State-dependent distance measure and approximations}
   867	
   868	We make extensive use of a state-dependent distance
   869	between measurements that has been frequently used in the context of
   870	entangled-prover interactive proof systems (see
   871	e.g.~\cite{IV12,ji2015classical}). For $\rho$ a positive semidefinite matrix and $X$ any linear operator define
   872	$$ \Trho(X) = \Tr(\rho X).$$ 
   873	For any two operators $S, T$, define the
   874	\emph{state-dependent distance} between $S$ an $T$ on a $\rho$ as
   875	$$ \Drho(S, T) := \sqrt{\Trho\big( (S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big)}.$$
   876	Based on the state-dependent distance we define a distance between POVMs, given by
   877	summing the state-dependent distance between the square roots of the POVM elements.
   878	Let $\{M^a\}$ and $\{N^a\}$ be two POVMs
   879	with the same number of outcomes, indexed by $a$, and let
   880	$\ket{\psi}$ be a quantum state. Then the state-dependent distance between the POVMs
   881	$M$ and $N$ on $\rho$ is denoted as $\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})$ and
   882	defined as
   883	\begin{align*}
   884	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}) = \Big(\sum_a \Drho\big(\sqrt{M^a}, \sqrt{N^a}\big)^2\Big)^{1/2}.
   885	\end{align*}
   886	While this notation is ambiguous (since the sum over outcomes is not explicitly
   887	indicated), context will always make it clear which notion of $\Drho$ is
   888	intended. We will also drop the square roots in the case of POVMs that are
   889	projective measurements.
   890	
   891	To simplify the notation, let $A^a = \sqrt{M^a}$ and $B^a =
   892	\sqrt{N^a}$. Then this distance can be rewritten as:
   893	\begin{align}
   894	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2 &= \sum_a \Trho\big( (A^a - B^a)^2 \rho\big) \notag\\
   895	               &= 2 - \sum_a \Re \Trho\big( A^a B^a \big),\label{eq:dpsi-1a}
   896	\end{align}
   897	where we  used the fact that $A^a$ and $B^a$ are
   898	Hermitian and their squares sum to identity. If we specialize to the case of projective measurements
   899	with binary outcomes, we get the following relations (here $A =
   900	A^1 - A^{-1}$ and $B = B^1 - B^{-1}$
   901	are the observables associated to the measurements):
   902	\begin{align}
   903	\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2  &= 2 - \Trho\big(A^{1} B^{1} + A^{-1} B^{-1} + B^{1} A^{1} + B^{-1}
   904	                 A^{-1}\big)  \nonumber \\
   905	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4} \Trho\big((\Id + A)(\Id + B)
   906	                 + (\Id - A)(\Id - B) + (\Id + B)(\Id + A)
   907	                 + (\Id  - B)(\Id - A)\big) \ket{\psi} \nonumber \\
   908	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4}\Trho\big(4\Id + 2 AB + 2 BA\big)\nonumber \\
   909	               &= 1 - \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big(AB + BA\big)  \nonumber \\
   910	               &= \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big((A - B)^2\big)\label{eq:dist_observables}    \\
   911	                &= \Drho(A, B)^2. \nonumber
   912	\end{align}
   913	This distance measure has the following useful property:
   914	
   915	\begin{lemma}
   916	  Let $\rho$ be positive semidefinite, $C$ be a linear operator such that $\|
   917	  CC^\dagger\| \leq K$ and $S, T$ linear operators. Then
   918	  $$\Big|\Trho (C S)- \Trho(CT ) \Big| \leq
   919	  \sqrt{2K} \Drho(S, T).$$
   920	
   921	  Likewise, if $\{C_a\}$ a family of operators such that $\|\sum_a C_aC_a^\dagger\|\leq K$ and $\{M^a\}$
   922	  and $\{N^a\}$ POVMs. Then 
   923	  $$\Big|\sum_a \Trho\big(  C_a \sqrt{M^a}\big) - \sum_a \Trho\big( C_a \sqrt{N^a}\big)\Big| \leq \sqrt{K}\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}).$$
   924	  \label{lem:approx}
   925	\end{lemma}
   926

   928	The proof of both results is identical, and uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality;
   929	we show only the proof of the second. Let $A^a = \sqrt{M^a}$ and $B^a = \sqrt{N^a}$. Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
   930	  \begin{align*}

  1061	
  1062	We state and analyze a variant of the classic 3-query linearity test of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld~\cite{BLR93} (BLR) that can be played with two entangled players. The two-player test is based on the idea of oracularization with a dummy question introduced in~\cite{IKM09}.  Our analysis builds on~\cite{IV12}, who analyze a $3$-player variant. Their proof is an extension of the Fourier-analytic proof due to H{\aa}stad to the matrix-valued setting. We analyze the two-player variant using similar techniques. 
  1063	
  1064	We note that the use of two players, rather than three as in
  1065	the original test, is essential for our applications to
  1066	self-testing. Ultimately we will require the provers to succeed in a linearity test performed in either of two mutually incompatible bases (e.g. the $X$ and $Z$ bases). Two provers
  1067	can achieve this by sharing a maximally entangled state, but there is no {tripartite} state that would allow three entangled provers to obtain consistent answers whenever they measure their share of the state in either the $X$ or the $Z$ basis. (Formulated differently, $\sigma_X\otimes \sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Z\otimes \sigma_Z$ share a common $+1$ eigenvector, the EPR pair; $\sigma_X\otimes \sigma_X \otimes \sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Z\otimes \sigma_Z \otimes \sigma_Z$ do not. This is a manifestation of entanglement monogamy.)
  1068	
  1069	We show the result in two
  1070	steps. First we show that any set of quantum observables satisfying
  1071	linearity relations approximately in expectation can be ``rounded'' to a
  1072	nearby set of observables satisfying these relations exactly. 
  1073	
  1074	\begin{theorem}
  1075	  Suppose there exist observables $\{A(a)\}_{a\in
  1076	  \{0,1\}^n}$ in $\Obs(\mH)$ acting on a state
  1077	  $\rho \in \Density(\mH)$ such that 
  1078		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qblr-0}
  1079		\E_{a, b} \Trho\big( A(a) A(b) A(a+b)\big) \geq 1-\delta.
  1080		\end{equation}
  1081		Then there exists an extended state $\rho' = \rho \otimes
  1082	  \proj{\rm{anc}} \in \Density(\mH\otimes \mH')$ and observables $\{\cA(a)\}$ in $\Obs(\mH\otimes\mH')$ such that 
  1083		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qblr-1}
  1084		\cA(a) \cA(b) = \cA(a+b) \quad \forall a, b \in \{0, 1\}^n\qquad \text{and}\qquad \E_a
  1085	  \DIS_{\rho'} (\cA(a), A(a))^2 \leq\delta.
  1086		\end{equation}
  1087	\label{thm:qblr}
  1088	\end{theorem}
  1089	
  1090	Here, and throughout this paper, the notation $a + b$ denotes the
  1091	bitwise XOR of $a$ and $b$, i.e. the sum of $a$ and $b$ viewed
  1092	as elements of the additive group ${\mathbb{Z}}_2^n$. We call observables
  1093	$\{\cA(a)\}$ satisfying the first set of relations in~\eqref{eq:qblr-1} \emph{exactly linear}.
  1094	
  1095	\begin{proof}
  1096	For every $u\in\{0,1\}^n$ consider the Fourier transform  $\hat{A}^u =
  1097	\E_{a} (-1)^{a\cdot u} A(a)$. Define measurement operators
  1098	  $B^u = (\hat{A}^u)^2$.
  1099	By Parseval's identity, these operators form a POVM. Using Naimark's theorem there exists an ancilla space $\mH'$, $\proj{\rm anc}\in\Density(\mH')$, and a projective
  1100	measurement $\{C^u\}$ on $\mH\otimes \mH'$ that simulates $\{B^u\}$. Introduce 
  1101	observables
  1102	\[ \cA(a) = \sum_{u} (-1)^{u\cdot a} C^u. \]
  1103	From the orthogonality of the projectors $C^u$ it follows that $\cA(a)
  1104	\cA(b) = \cA(a+b)$. Write 
  1105	\begin{align*}
  1106	  \E_{a} \CON_{\rho'}(A(a), \cA(a))
  1107	  &= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\E_{a}\Re\Tr_{\rho'}\big( A(a)\cA(a)\big)\\
  1108		&= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\E_{a}\Re\Big(\sum_u \Trho\big( (-1)^{u\cdot a} A(a)(\hat{A}^u)^2\big)\Big)\\

  1112	  $\sum_u \Trho((\hat{A}^u)^3) =\E_{ab} \Trho(A(a) A(b) A(a + b))$, and use the assumption made in the theorem and the relation between $\CON_{\rho'}$ and $\DIS_{\rho'}^2 $.

item.text: The normalization note’s counterexample is mathematically viable: exact Boolean representations decompose into characters, so an ancillary extension cannot beat its lower bound. The main remaining risk is therefore implementation-level: whether the Fourier identities, trace normalization, and residual-outcome absorption prove exactly the advertised contracts without hidden proof debt or avoidable API/style problems.

    97	% statement below carries the corrected operator bound together with the
    98	% equivalent measurement form. The mirror's quotation

   101	% together with the exact linearity, under the quantifier "for all u, u' in
